9. In the above case, the Appellate Division upheld the view of the High Court Division stating that under section 439 of the CrPC is the only option to prefer revision by the petitioner against the order of acquittal. Because, the petitioner could not file an appeal under section 417(2)(a) of the CrPC within sixty days from the date of order of acquittal as prescribed in section 417(3) of the CrPC. In the present case in hand, same incident took place with regard to prefer an appeal. Apart from this, if the limitation of filing appeal was not expired, then the revision would have been more applicable because the question of legal evidence of the witnesses and unsigned notice is involved in the case, not error of law. 

 10. Now the second question is whether unsigned legal notice shuts down the prosecution case. The trial judge observed that the legal notice served by the petitioner to the accused-opposite party No.2 was not signed. This is also one of the reasons to pass an order of acquittal, As per section 138(1)(b) of the Act, 1881, the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, is to make a demand for the payment of the amount by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within thirty days from the date of receipt of information by him from the bank regarding return of the cheque unpaid. In this provision there is no indication about the legal notice to compulsorily be signed by the sender. In the present case, the holder of the cheque i.e the petitioner according to this provision sent the legal notice through his engaged lawyer to the drawer of the cheque after getting information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque unpaid within thirty days. But the legal notice was not signed mistakenly by the learned Advocate as observed by the judge of the trial court. In this respect a reference may be made to the case of India Kumar Patodia and ors. vs Reliance Industries Ltd. and others reported in MANU/SC/1012/2012 in which two points were placed before the Supreme Court of India, whether the complaint without the signature of the complainant, in, spite of verification of complaint, is "non-entia" and whether no prosecution can lie on such complaint; and whether it is mere irregularity and it can be cured subsequently and whether such subsequent amendment would relate back to the date of filing of the complaint or whether it would hit by the law of limitation. The Supreme Court of India observed that no prejudice has been caused to the accused for non-signing the complaint because of the fact that the statement made on oath and signed by the complainant safeguards the interest of the accused and further held that the requirements of section 142(a) of the Act is that the complaint must necessarily be in writing and the complaint can be presented by the payee or holder in due course of the cheque and it need not be signed by the complainant.
